newsitem.title: USA: Wis. audit says bond deals over 3 yrs reasonable.
newsitem.headline: Wis. audit says bond deals over 3 yrs reasonable.

text.p: Wisconsin bonds have been issued at reasonable interest rates over the past three years and the average costs for the competitive and negotiated deals "compare favorably" to other states, a legislative audit bureau review has found.

Wisconsin lawmakers sought the audit in April after Democrats raised concerns that donations by securities firms to the state Republican Party may have influenced the selection of underwriters for negotiated deals.

The audit bureau report released Wednesday found Wisconsin's use of requests for proposal "fair and equitable" for selecting underwriters, but raised concerns that three of eight score sheets ranking the applications by the Capital Finance Office could not be located.

Sen. Robert Wirch, D-Kenosha, co-chair of the legislative joint audit committee, said Thursday the review satisfied questions about the competitive sales, but did not resolve issues on the negotiated deals.
Audit Committee co-chair Rep. Mary Lazich, R-New Berlin, said, however, the audit found "no improprieties or favoritism" and fully satisfied her concerns.
Wisconsin has made fewer negotiated sales than other states and used a good process looking out for the public interest, Lazich said.
Wirch contended the audit found no established procedure for negotiated deals, missing slips and some unqualified evaluators reviewing underwriters.
"I think there is cause for concern about the process, but clearly there is no evidence of wrongdoing and I think that is the message from the audit," Wirch said.
"If there was wrongdoing, it is something that was not detectable in this audit, but there should have been a better process out there in the negotiated bond process," Wirch said.
Former state Administration Department Secretary James Klauser, who oversaw the debt issuances during the period, called the questions raised political and said the audit resolved the matter.

"Other than the politics of false accusations, which seems to be the characteristic of the day unfortunately, an independent review by the audit bureau and an earlier action by the ethics board last week totally validates the process and should, on the merits, bring closure," Klauser said.
No evidence has shown that contributions led to more bond deals and "the company that allegedly made the greatest contribution, got the least amount of work," Klauser said.
Wisconsin sold $1.8 billion of bonds from January 1994 through April of this year in 15 competitive and five negotiated deals.
Eight different lead underwriters participated in the deals earning $5.7 million of profits from competitive issues totalling $1.4 billion and $2.9 million from negotiated issues of $440.3 million.
Two firms handled more than half the negotiated bonds with Merrill Lynch & Co selling $151 million and Bear, Stearns & Co Inc more than $93 million.
And 98 firms participated in the competitive bid process.
